hints: Start from the stem - what exactly has changed in the beta-globin chain? Focus on the R group property of the new amino acid compared to the old one.
Think about how a non-polar patch on the surface of one HbS molecule could interact with a non-polar patch on a neighbouring HbS molecule at low oxygen.
walkthrough:
Link Mutation to Primary Structure**
You are told glutamine with a polar R group is replaced by valine with a non-polar R group. That is a change in amino acid sequence, so the primary structure of beta-globin is altered. Remember primary structure determines all later folding and interactions.

From Hydrophobic Patch to Fibres**
Valine exposes a non-polar, hydrophobic patch on the surface of HbS. Hydrophobic patches avoid water by sticking to each other, so at low $p\text{O}_2$ bonds form between HbS molecules. Many molecules joining together is what we see as fibres.

Final answer: The primary structure is changed, polar glutamine replaced by non-polar valine. The non-polar R groups form different bonds between HbS molecules, causing them to stick together as fibres.

hints: With British-198, an adult still has up to 20% HbF alongside HbS instead of less than 1%. How would having two types of haemoglobin in the same red cell affect HbS concentration?
Use the last bullet point - HbF holds onto oxygen more strongly at low $p\text{O}_2$. How would avoiding very low oxygen inside the cell affect fibre formation?
walkthrough:
Dilution Effect of HbF**
British-198 keeps fetal genes switched on, so about 20% of haemoglobin is HbF and only about 80% is HbS. With less HbS per cell, HbS molecules meet each other less often, so fibre formation and shape change are decreased.

High Affinity Keeps Oxygen Loaded**
Fibres only form at low $p\text{O}_2$ when haemoglobin is deoxygenated. HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen at low $p\text{O}_2$ than adult haemoglobin, so blood and tissues avoid reaching the very low $p\text{O}_2$ that triggers sickling. Fewer sickled cells means fewer blocked capillaries and reduced symptoms.

Final answer: Both HbF and HbS are present, diluting HbS. HbF with high oxygen affinity avoids very low $p\text{O}_2$, so less HbS shape change / fibre formation, fewer cells sickle and block capillaries.

hints: Recall the general name for any protein that binds DNA to switch genes on or off in eukaryotes.
walkthrough:
Naming the Gene Switch Protein**
Genes are switched on or off when a specific protein binds to DNA near the gene and controls transcription. The syllabus term for this is a transcription factor, also accepted as a regulatory protein.

hints: All haemoglobins are made negative by alkaline buffer. If they are placed in an electric field, which electrode will they move toward?
HbS has an extra positive charge compared to HbA. How will that change its overall negative charge and its speed?
Think about what slower movement means for distance travelled in a fixed time on the gel.
To diagnose, you cannot use distance alone - what must you compare the patient bands with, and what pattern would prove sickle cell anaemia?
walkthrough:
Setting Up Movement to the Anode**
Alkaline buffer gives all haemoglobin molecules a net negative charge. When a current and potential difference is applied across the gel, an electric field is created and negative proteins are attracted to and move toward the anode, the positive electrode.

Why HbS Lags Behind**
HbS carries an additional positive charge compared to HbA, so its net negative charge is smaller. A smaller net charge means a weaker attraction and slower migration, so in the same time HbS travels a shorter distance from the negative end than HbA.

Reading the Diagnosis**
You run the sample alongside known HbA, HbF and HbS or a reference lane and compare band positions. A normal person shows mainly HbA, a carrier shows two bands, and if only a single band is seen at the HbS position the person has sickle cell anaemia with only HbS.

Final answer: Apply current / potential difference across gel; negatively charged Hb moves to anode / positive electrode. HbS is more positive so moves more slowly / shorter distance from negative end. Compare bands to known / reference haemoglobins; single band at HbS position indicates sickle cell anaemia.

hints: Use lane 1 (only HbA) and lane 5 (HbA top, HbF middle, HbS bottom) as a ruler. What haemoglobins would a one-month-old normal baby still contain?
Remember SCT means both HbA and HbS genes are present, while sickle cell anaemia means all adult haemoglobin is HbS. How many bands will each show and at which positions?
walkthrough:
Use the Reference to Place Bands**
Lane 5 tells you the order from the wells: HbA furthest, then HbF, then HbS shortest. Lane 1 confirms normal adult is a single HbA band.

Predict Each Lane**
Lane 2 is a one-month-old normal baby, so adult HbA has started but much HbF remains - draw two bands at HbA and HbF. Lane 3 is SCT, heterozygous $Hb^A Hb^S$, so both proteins are made - draw two bands at HbA and HbS. Lane 4 is sickle cell anaemia with only HbS adult haemoglobin - draw one band only at the HbS position.

Final answer: Lane 2 (one-month-old normal): bands at HbA and HbF positions. Lane 3 (SCT, HbA HbS heterozygote): bands at HbA and HbS positions. Lane 4 (sickle cell anaemia): single band at HbS position only.
